common_name: Wizard Rose Coleus (Compact Rose-Pink Seed-Grown Coleus)

planting.note: Start seed indoors or plant after all frost danger has passed; Wizard Rose is a compact, seed-grown Wizard series coleus with rose-pink leaves centered in maroon, uniform from seed and tolerant of both sun and shade.

directions: Plant in partial shade to nearly full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix, spacing plants close together for a solid, uniform bedding effect. Wizard Rose bears rose-pink leaves with a deep maroon center blotch on a compact, mounded plant that grows true from seed, making it a dependable choice for mass plantings and municipal beds. Its soft pink tone brightens shaded borders and pairs well with white- or silver-leaved companions. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to keep the plant's energy directed into foliage color, and shear lightly in midsummer if plants become leggy.
sources: Ball Horticultural Company — Wizard coleus series notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Coleus as Annual Foliage Plant

common_name: Kong Salmon Pink Coleus (Giant Salmon-Rose Shade Coleus)

planting.note: Start seed indoors or plant container plants after the last frost in moist, rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Kong Salmon Pink bears huge, palm-sized leaves in salmon-rose with darker rose veining, needing protection from hot afternoon sun.

directions: Plant in moist, rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, keeping soil consistently moist since the Kong series' oversized leaves wilt quickly if allowed to dry out. Kong Salmon Pink bears exceptionally large, heart-shaped leaves in a soft salmon-rose overlaid with darker rose veining, giving a gentler color statement than the deep burgundy Kong Red. Its bold scale and pastel tone make it a striking textural anchor massed in a shaded bed or in a large container alongside ferns and hostas. Pinch flower spikes as they appear to keep energy directed into leaf growth, and pinch growing tips occasionally for a fuller habit.
sources: Ball Horticultural Company — Kong coleus series notes

common_name: Kong Lime Vein Coleus (Giant Chartreuse Green-Veined Shade Coleus)

planting.note: Start seed indoors or plant container plants after the last frost in moist, rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Kong Lime Vein bears huge, palm-sized chartreuse leaves traced with contrasting deep-green veining, brightening the darkest corners of the shade garden.

directions: Plant in moist, rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, and keep soil consistently moist, since the Kong series' enormous leaves wilt quickly in dry conditions. Kong Lime Vein bears exceptionally large, bright chartreuse leaves overlaid with a fine network of deep-green veins, one of the palest, most luminous colors in the Kong series and a strong choice for lighting up deep shade. Its glowing color and huge scale make a bold textural statement massed in a shaded bed or as a specimen in a large container, pairing well with dark-leaved companions for contrast. Pinch flower spikes as they appear to keep energy directed into leaf growth, and pinch growing tips periodically for a fuller habit.
sources: Ball Horticultural Company — Kong coleus series notes

common_name: Copper Countess Coleus (Heirloom Trailing Copper-Orange Coleus)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Copper Countess is an heirloom trailing coleus with small, rounded leaves in warm copper-orange, useful for spilling over the edges of pots and hanging baskets.

directions: Plant in partial shade to morning sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix, giving the trailing stems room to cascade. Copper Countess is an old, long-grown heirloom coleus with small, rounded leaves in a warm, uniform copper-orange, kept in circulation for generations by coleus collectors and specialty growers for its trailing, low-mounding habit. It excels spilling over the rim of a hanging basket or window box, or as a groundcover-like filler at the front of a shaded bed. Pinch stem tips regularly to encourage branching and a fuller cascade, and remove flower spikes as they appear to keep foliage color strong.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Gardening Portal, Coleus
coleus collector nursery records (Rosy Dawn Gardens, NCCC coleus trials)

common_name: India Frills Coleus (Classic Ruffled Burgundy-and-Chartreuse Coleus)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; India Frills is a classic named coleus with deeply cut, ruffled leaf margins in burgundy centers edged bright chartreuse, grown for its distinctive lacy texture.

directions: Plant in partial shade to filtered sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix. India Frills carries deeply lobed, heavily ruffled leaves with dark burgundy centers and a wide, irregular chartreuse edge, a texture that sets it apart from smoother-leaved coleus cultivars and has kept it popular among collectors for decades. Its frilled foliage reads as fine, lacy texture from a distance and as bold color up close, making it a good textural counterpoint to broad-leaved hostas or ferns. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to redirect energy into foliage, and pinch stem tips periodically to keep the plant full and well branched.
sources: coleus collector nursery records (Rosy Dawn Gardens, NCCC coleus trials)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Merlin's Magic bears creamy white leaves with an irregular green margin, one of the palest coleus cultivars available, useful for brightening dim corners of the shade garden.

directions: Plant in partial to full shade in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix; too much direct sun can scorch the pale leaf tissue. Merlin's Magic bears near-white leaves edged in a narrow band of green, giving it one of the lightest, most luminous color patterns in the coleus world and making it especially effective for illuminating deeply shaded beds at dusk. Its ghostly foliage pairs beautifully with dark-leaved heucheras or black-flowered companions for high contrast. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to keep the plant's energy directed into foliage, and pinch growing tips periodically to maintain a bushy, well-branched habit.
sources: coleus collector nursery records (Rosy Dawn Gardens, NCCC coleus trials)
North Carolina State Extension — Gardening Portal, Coleus

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Defiance is an older named cultivar with broad maroon leaves edged in a band of glowing red-orange, a long-cultivated bedding coleus prized for its strong, saturated color.

directions: Plant in partial shade to morning sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix. Defiance carries broad, deep maroon leaves rimmed in a band of glowing red-orange, a long-cultivated bedding cultivar valued for its bold, saturated color and reliable, well-branched habit. It holds its color well through summer heat and works effectively as a mid-border accent among green- or gold-leaved companions. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to keep the plant's energy directed into foliage, and pinch growing tips periodically to encourage a fuller, bushier form.
sources: coleus collector nursery records (Rosy Dawn Gardens, NCCC coleus trials)

common_name: Fairway Rose Coleus (Dwarf Seed-Grown Bedding Coleus)

planting.note: Start seed indoors or plant after all frost danger has passed; Fairway Rose is part of an older, dwarf seed-grown bedding series with small rose-pink leaves on compact, uniform plants suited to edging and mass plantings.

directions: Plant in partial shade to nearly full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix, spacing plants closely for a dense, uniform bedding display. Fairway Rose belongs to an older dwarf seed strain bred for small stature and even germination, bearing compact rose-pink leaves on tidy, mounded plants only a few inches tall. Its diminutive size makes it well suited to edging walkways, window boxes, and small-scale plantings where larger coleus cultivars would overwhelm the space. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to keep the plant's energy directed into foliage color.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Coleus as Annual Foliage Plant
Ball Horticultural Company — historical seed coleus series notes

common_name: ColorBlaze Rustic Orange Coleus (Mounding Orange Dark-Veined Coleus)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Rustic Orange, part of the ColorBlaze series, bears burnt-orange leaves traced with darker maroon veining on a well-branched, mounding plant tolerant of sun and shade.

directions: Plant in a spot with morning sun and afternoon shade, or filtered light all day, in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix; more direct sun deepens the warm tones while deep shade can dull the color. Rustic Orange, part of the ColorBlaze series, bears burnt-orange leaves overlaid with darker maroon veining, giving it a warm, autumnal look that holds from summer into fall. Its steady, mounded habit and season-long color make it an effective warm-toned accent paired with purple or chartreuse companions in beds and large containers. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to keep the plant's energy directed into foliage, and pinch growing tips periodically for a fuller habit.

common_name: Main Street Broadway Coleus (Bold Burgundy-and-Green Sun Coleus)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Broadway, part of the street-themed Main Street series, bears bold, broad leaves in burgundy and green bred for strong performance in full sun as well as shade.

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix; the Main Street series was bred for garden performance across a wide range of light conditions. Broadway bears bold, broad leaves patterned in burgundy and green, forming a vigorous, well-branched plant that holds its color and shape through summer heat. Its adaptability to both sun and shade makes it a versatile choice for mixed borders, foundation plantings, or large container combinations. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to keep the plant's energy directed into foliage, and pinch growing tips periodically to maintain a full, bushy habit.
sources: Ball Horticultural Company — Main Street coleus series notes
North Carolina State Extension — Gardening Portal, Coleus
